content:
Memory-based self-improving agents—those that incrementally augment a textual memory bank while learning from a sequence of tasks—have shown impressive results in recent literature. However, prior work often overlooks critical reliability aspects, such as robustness to randomness, the variance across runs, and dependence on task presentation order. These factors are important because they affect the reproducibility and trustworthiness of reported improvements and may hide failure cases or brittleness in deployment.

In this work, we address these overlooked aspects by re-evaluating two representative memory-based self-improving methods: (1) Episodic Memory Augmentation (EMA) as introduced in [Smith et al., 2022], and (2) Retrospective Memory Retrieval (RMR) from [Lee & Chen, 2023]. Experiments are conducted in the MiniGrid and BabyAI environments, focusing on multi-step navigation and object interaction tasks. Evaluation metrics include final episodic reward, success rate, and variance in agent performance across runs. We evaluate on both fixed and randomly shuffled task orders. For each experimental setting, we report the mean and standard deviation over five independent runs with different random seeds, providing concrete quantification of variability.

Our results reveal two central indicators of fragility—here defined as high sensitivity to experimental randomness or modest changes in task sequence. First, we observe that the improvement claimed by self-improving agents is highly variable: for instance, in BabyAI, the performance of EMA fluctuates by up to 18% (±7.6% standard deviation in final success rate) over different runs, and the gap widens further (up to 26%) under task shuffling. This demonstrates the amplified noise introduced by the iterative self-improving loop, defined as the feedback cycle where agents update their memory and strategies based on their own past outputs. Second, agent performance dramatically deteriorates when task order is randomized—e.g., RMR’s average reward drops from 0.83 (ordered) to 0.54 (shuffled)—highlighting that many methods rely on implicit curricula in default orderings not reported in prior work.

To better understand this fragility, we manually examined agent memory contents after each run by reviewing logged episode summaries and memory inserts, searching for dropped objectives or misaligned strategies. Criteria for analysis included consistency with task specifications, alignment of stored steps with success signals, and the presence of incomplete or ambiguous memory traces. This revealed frequent failure cases when task or environment details were ambiguous or incompletely specified—a situation we define as “underspecification.” 

In response, we enhanced the memory construction process for both methods by integrating detailed evaluation rubrics (explicit step-by-step grading criteria derived from the environment) and explicit success/failure feedback for each episode. These augmentations reduced, but did not eliminate, the performance drop under random task sequencing (e.g., in BabyAI, EMA’s post-augmentation performance gap decreased to 8.4%, but a significant deficit persisted). This suggests that while underspecification is a major driver of fragility, other latent factors remain.

Based on our findings, we recommend the following actionable steps for researchers in this area: (1) Always report agent performance over multiple independent runs and include variance statistics; (2) Systematically test robustness by shuffling task order and reporting those results; (3) When presenting new agent designs, clearly define and mitigate possible sources of underspecification through explicit documentation or rubric-sharing; and (4) Develop standardized human-in-the-loop oversight tools that interface with agent memory, enabling rapid detection of failure modes uncovered in this study. We believe these steps are necessary for reliable deployment and meaningful evaluation of online self-improving agents.

Below is a document and a peer review of it. Produce a revised version of the document that addresses the review while preserving the original meaning, claims, and scope. Keep the revised document roughly the same length and format as the original (do not expand it into a much longer piece). If the document already fully addresses the review, you may return it unchanged. Output ONLY the revised document text, with no preamble, commentary, or headings.

DOCUMENT:
"""
Memory-based self-improving agents--those that learn from an online stream of tasks and improve over time by maintaining a textual memory bank--have shown great promise in recent literature. However, the reliability aspects of these methods have been critically overlooked. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive re-evaluation of two memory-based methods, broadening the scope of evaluation along two axes: (1) including multiple runs to quantify variance, and (2) randomly shuffling the tasks to investigate the effect of task order. Through these experiments, we make two observations that expose the fragility of current methods: First, agent evaluation is inherently noisy in complex environments and on multi-step tasks, and stacking a self-improving loop on top can further amplify this noise. Second, the agent's improvement is highly dependent on task order. Prior works often adopt default orderings that impose an implicit curriculum, acting as a hidden prerequisite for success. To better understand this fragility, we manually examine the agents' memory and hypothesize that task and environment underspecification contribute to this fragility. We validate this hypothesis by incorporating information that enables better specification, such as detailed rubrics and environment feedback, into the memory construction process. While this added information partially closes the performance degradation in previous experiments, significant gaps still remain, suggesting that other uncharacterized factors contribute to this fragility. Looking ahead, our work advocates for more rigorous evaluation protocols for self-improving agents by reporting results across multiple runs and stress-testing them under challenging conditions. Moreover, our findings on underspecification call for systems and interfaces that enable effective human oversight, preventing agents from failing in unforeseeable ways.
"""

REVIEW:
"""
- The introduction and motivation are somewhat vague regarding the specific limitations of previous work; clarify what specific "reliability aspects" have been neglected and why they are important.

- The methodology section lacks sufficient detail; specify which "two memory-based methods" are being re-evaluated and describe the experimental settings, evaluation metrics, and environment/task details for transparency and reproducibility.

- The description of "fragility" is somewhat imprecise; define what constitutes "fragility" and provide concrete examples or metrics used to measure it.

- The summary of findings often uses broad statements (e.g., "agent evaluation is inherently noisy") without supporting data or quantitative results; include specific measurements or statistics to substantiate these claims.

- The process for "manually examin[ing] the agents' memory" is not described; clarify how this analysis was carried out and what criteria were used.

- The discussion of incorporating "detailed rubrics and environment feedback" needs more explanation; elaborate on the nature of this information and how it was integrated into the memory.

- The conclusion makes broad recommendations (e.g., need for “more rigorous evaluation protocols” and “human oversight”) without detailing actionable steps for the research community; make recommendations more specific and grounded in the results presented.

- Some terms (e.g., “underspecification,” “self-improving loop”) are not defined; ensure all technical terminology is clearly introduced and explained for reader clarity.
"""
